Elizabeth Cady Stanton. The American women's rights pioneer whose Declaration of Sentiments at the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention became the manifesto of the women's movement.

Stanton drafted and presented this declaration, modeling it on the Declaration of Independence but listing the grievances of women against men's laws and customs. The declaration's demand for women's suffrage was controversial even among other women's rights supporters. It was in fact the only resolution at Seneca Falls that was not unanimously passed.

She co-founded and led the National Woman Suffrage Association alongside Susan B. Anthony, and together they shaped the movement's strategy and ideology for fifty years. Stanton wrote extensively on women's equality, religious critique, and the connections between women's rights and other reform movements—labor rights, abolition, temperance. She argued that women's oppression was not separate from these struggles but intertwined with them.

She did not live to see the Nineteenth Amendment. She died in 1902, eighteen years before women gained the federal vote. But late in her life, she collaborated with Susan B. Anthony and Matilda Joslyn Gage on The History of Woman Suffrage, ensuring that the movement's record and ideology would survive for generations to come.
